methods.label: Match the symmetric-power and cosine recurrences
methods.explanation:
The domain of \(x\) matters. The reciprocal requires \(x\ne0\), so multiplying the premise by \(x\) gives
\[
x^2-2\cos\theta\,x+1=0,
\]
or, using \(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1\),
\[
(x-\cos\theta)^2+\sin^2\theta=0.
\]
Because \(0<\theta<\pi\), we have \(\sin\theta>0\). Thus no real \(x\) satisfies the premise.

For the following calculation, assume that \(x\) is allowed to be complex. The quadratic then has the nonzero roots \(\cos\theta\pm i\sin\theta\), where \(i^2=-1\), so this interpretation does provide admissible values.

The given reciprocal sum suggests grouping higher powers in the same way. Define
\[
S_m=x^m+x^{-m}\qquad(m=0,1,2,\ldots).
\]
The initial values are \(S_0=2\) and \(S_1=2\cos\theta\). For \(m\ge1\), expanding a product gives
\[
(x+x^{-1})S_m=S_{m+1}+S_{m-1}.
\]
Therefore
\[
S_{m+1}=2\cos\theta\,S_m-S_{m-1}.
\]
This recurrence reduces each higher symmetric power to the preceding two.

The cosine addition and subtraction formulas give
\[
\cos((m+1)\theta)+\cos((m-1)\theta)
=2\cos\theta\cos(m\theta).
\]
Hence \(T_m=2\cos(m\theta)\) obeys exactly the same recurrence, with \(T_0=2\) and \(T_1=2\cos\theta\). If two consecutive \(S\)-values equal their corresponding \(T\)-values, the recurrence makes the next values equal as well. Starting from indices \(0\) and \(1\), induction proves
\[
x^n+\frac1{x^n}=\boxed{2\cos(n\theta)}
\]
for every positive integer \(n\). This is choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\) under the complex-domain interpretation. Over the reals, the premise has no solutions.
